summary: Root cause (high confidence, 0.78): the shared PostgreSQL datastore ledger-db exhausted its data volume on /var/lib/postgresql/data, with WAL retained by an inactive replication slot, and every writer on that datastore surfaced "No space left on device" write failures. This is strongly supported: disk-pressure warnings began at 13:10Z (~1.5h before the only change in the window, payment-service v6.0.0 at 14:46Z), ledger-db itself logged internal storage-exhaustion PANICs on pg_wal and data files at 15:01Z, and order-service — which received no deployment and never writes MANDATE_HOLD — failed with the identical storage error in the same minute. payment-service v6.0.0 is best explained as a temporal coincidence (possibly a minor, innocent contributor to write volume), not the origin of the fault; the reported "new ledger entry type" theory is rejected on mechanism and scope. The rollback of v6.0.0 at 15:12Z did not restore service because it did not touch the exhausted shared volume.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Independent ledger-db storage exhaustion (inactive replication slot retaining WAL) fills the disk; all four writer services fail
ranked_hypotheses.statement: ledger-db, the shared postgres backing ledger writes, ran out of disk on /var/lib/postgresql/data because an inactive replication slot retained WAL. Disk crossed 90% at 13:10Z and 98% at 14:48Z, then hard-failed at ~15:01Z with PANICs writing pg_wal and extending data files. Every writer on the shared datastore — payment-service, order-service (and likely portfolio/settlement) — surfaced 'No space left on device' write failures within the same minute. payment-service v6.0.0 is a temporal coincidence plus a plausible innocent contributor of a small amount of extra write volume, not the origin of the fault.

causal_chain.claim: Inactive replication slot retains WAL on ledger-db, consuming disk persistently from at least 13:02Z
Disk utilisation climbs 90% (13:10Z) → 95% (14:15Z) → 98% (14:48Z) on the data volume
Disk hits full: PANICs 'could not write to file pg_wal/xlogtemp' (15:01:01Z) and 'could not extend file base/...' (15:01:39Z)
All clients of the shared datastore get 'No space left on device' on their writes — payment-service 'ledger write failed: ERROR: could not extend file' at 15:00:26Z
order-service fails independently with 'INSERT INTO orders failed: No space left on device' at 15:00:42Z, proving the blast radius is the shared store, not the payment code path
payment-service error rate jumps from ~0.2% to ~60% in the 15:00Z bucket and stays there; the mandate flow is one of many writers affected

assumptions: The disk-pressure WARNs and WAL-retention warnings originate from the same inactive replication slot mechanism as HIST-114 (the log wording matches but the slot identity was not directly read)
The 15:00 bucket boundary hides a sub-minute onset; the true head of the causal chain is the disk fill, which predates it by ~2 hours
ledger-db disk capacity/occupancy was a genuine exhausted-volume rather than a quota/permission error (message text says No space left on device)

ranked_hypotheses.title: Rollback of payment-service is masking a still-broken shared datastore; the fault predates and outlives the deploy
ranked_hypotheses.statement: payment-service v6.0.0 was rolled back at 15:12Z, ~12 minutes after onset, but the ledger-db disk exhaustion that actually causes the write failures is untouched by that rollback. If failures persist after 15:12Z, it confirms the origin is ledger-db's exhausted storage, not the release. This is a discriminator-framing hypothesis about the intervention evidence rather than a separate origin, and it converges on ledger-db resource exhaustion.

causal_chain.claim: ledger-db begins disk-pressure warnings at 13:10Z and WAL-retention warnings from 13:02Z, well before any deploy
payment-service v6.0.0 deploys 14:46Z and is rolled back 15:12Z, but the underlying volume stays full
payment-service error rate stays 59-64% through the end of the window (16:59Z), past the 15:12Z rollback
order-service, which received no change at all, is failing with the same storage error from 15:00:42Z, so removing payment v6.0.0 cannot restore writes

assumptions: Error rate after 15:12Z is at least partly attributable to the same storage failure rather than a clean recovery delayed by in-flight retries (the bucket data shows sustained 59-64%, which favours persistence)
No disk-reclamation intervention occurred between 15:12Z and 16:59Z

ranked_hypotheses.title: payment-service v6.0.0 mandate flow's new MANDATE_HOLD write pattern amplified ledger-db pressure and triggered the disk exhaustion
ranked_hypotheses.statement: The v6.0.0 deploy at 14:46Z introduced a new UPI mandate flow whose MANDATE_HOLD ledger entries (and possibly retry-on-error behaviour) materially increased write volume / WAL generation against ledger-db, pushing an already-nearly-full disk over the edge ~14 minutes later. Without the extra writes the disk would not have filled in this window. The fault origin is the payment-service release, but the visible failure is storage exhaustion on a shared dependency.

causal_chain.claim: ledger-db disk is already high (90% at 13:10Z) before any deploy — a pre-existing, non-deploy condition
payment-service v6.0.0 (new UPI mandate flow, new MANDATE_HOLD entry type) deploys at 14:46Z — the only change in the entire window
The new mandate flow writes extra/novel ledger entries, accelerating WAL generation and data growth on the already-tight volume
Disk reaches 98% at 14:48Z (~2 min after deploy) and hard-fails at 15:00-15:01Z
payment-service errors at 15:00:26Z with the storage error, and the 14:46Z deploy sits ~14 min before the 15:00Z onset

assumptions: v6.0.0's mandate flow measurably increased ledger-db write volume — no insert-rate or write-volume metric was ever retrieved (explicit GAP)
The 98% reading at 14:48Z reflects accelerated fill rather than the same slow trajectory continuing from 13:10Z
order-service's simultaneous failure is collateral (contention on the exhausted volume) rather than independent evidence that the trigger is elsewhere

ranked_hypotheses.title: v6.0.0's new MANDATE_HOLD entry type was rejected by ledger-db schema/enum (or a missing migration), producing ledger write failures
ranked_hypotheses.statement: The new ledger entry type MANDATE_HOLD is not accepted by the ledger-db schema or enum because the corresponding schema migration/registration was never deployed; the write path fails on the type itself and payment-service surfaces the failure as 'ledger write failed'. This is the reporter's stated suspicion and the orchestrator's second theory, both of which name ledger-db as the fault site.

causal_chain.claim: v6.0.0 introduces a new ledger entry type MANDATE_HOLD
No schema migration, enum registration or config change was deployed for ledger-db in the window, so the new value is unregistered
ledger-db rejects the unrecognised entry type, returning an error that payment-service wraps as 'ledger write failed'
payment-service error rate reaches ~60% from the 15:00Z bucket

assumptions: An unregistered enum value would surface as a storage 'No space left on device' error — which is the opposite of what such a rejection would look like
Non-payment writers would also fail for the same reason (they cannot, since they do not write MANDATE_HOLD — yet order-service failed identically)
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: Mechanism mismatch and scope mismatch. The dominant error (354 occurrences) is a storage error — 'could not extend file: No space left on device' — not a type/enum/constraint violation; no app-exception, schema or type error pattern is present (F8). ledger-db's own logs show internal storage exhaustion PANICs (F10). order-service, which never writes MANDATE_HOLD, fails identically and simultaneously (F11), which a type-rejection mechanism cannot explain. No 'new ledger entry type' root cause exists in any historical incident, while the disk-full/WAL precedent matches exactly (F17, F18).

facts.statement: The dominant payment-service error is a downstream storage failure: 354 occurrences of 'ledger write failed: ERROR: could not extend file: No space left on device', first seen 2026-06-01T15:00:26Z; there is no dominant timeout, auth, or app-exception pattern.

ledger-db showed disk pressure well before payment-service errors: 90% on /var/lib/postgresql/data at 13:10:01Z, 95% at 14:15:45Z, 98% at 14:48:20Z, plus repeated inactive-replication-slot WAL retention warnings from 13:02:25Z; hard write failures followed at 15:01:01Z.

ledger-db's own logs show internal storage exhaustion PANICs: 153 'could not write to file "pg_wal/xlogtemp.<n>": No space left on device' (first 15:01:01Z) and 139 'could not extend file "base/<n>/<n>": No space left on device' (first 15:01:39Z).

order-service independently produced 236 occurrences of 'INSERT INTO orders failed: No space left on device' (first_seen 2026-06-01T15:00:42Z), the same storage error in the same minute as payment-service, indicating a shared-storage blast radius rather than a payment-specific bug.
ledger-db is a shared postgres (owner platform, shared: true) with four writer services — order-service, portfolio-service, payment-service and settlement-service all hold db edges to it.

Exactly one deployment occurred in 12:00-16:59Z: dep-6203 payment-service v6.0.0 'New UPI mandate flow' (changes include 'new ledger entry type MANDATE_HOLD'), deployed 2026-06-01T14:46:00Z, rolled back at 2026-06-01T15:12:00Z — i.e. after the 13:10Z start of disk pressure and ~14 min before the 15:00Z onset.
No config or feature-flag changes were recorded for any service in 12:00-16:59Z (count 0); the change surface is deploy-only.
No deployment and no config change was ever recorded for ledger-db (count 0 for both over 2026-05-25T00:00Z-2026-06-01T16:59Z), so no DB-side migration or schema change exists in the window.

payment-service error rate sat at baseline ~0.19-0.29% through the 14:56:00Z bucket, then jumped to avg 60.15% / max 60.8% in the 15:00:00Z bucket and stayed 59-64% for the rest of the window — including well past the 15:12Z rollback.
There is no service named 'ledger-service' in the topology/release system; the only ledger component is the shared datastore ledger-db, so no ledger-side application deploy could have occurred.

Historical precedent matches this signature: HIST-114 (2025-04-18) 'ledger-db disk full from retained WAL' with symptoms 'no space left on device' / 'write failures', root cause 'Inactive replication slot retained WAL until disk filled'; no historical incident has a 'new ledger entry type' / enum / schema-migration root cause in the top matches.

assumptions: The inactive-replication-slot WAL retention warnings (from 13:02:25Z) and the disk-pressure WARNs originate from the same mechanism as historical incident HIST-114; the specific slot identity was not directly read in this investigation (log wording matches, slot name unverified).
The disk-full condition was a genuine exhausted-volume state rather than a quota or permission error, based on the 'No space left on device' message text.
The 240s error-rate bucket hides a sub-minute onset; the true head of the causal chain is the disk fill, which begins ~2 hours before the error onset.
The observed errors are the complete picture for the checked services; unexamined components (api-gateway, kafka, redis-cache, bank-partner-api) did not introduce an earlier independent failure.

(demoted from facts: no verified observation backs it) Ordering of onsets: ledger-db disk-pressure WARNs (13:10Z onward) precede payment-service errors, while ledger-db hard PANICs (15:01:01Z) are essentially simultaneous with payment-service's first error (15:00:26Z) and order-service's first error (15:00:42Z).

timeline.event: Repeated inactive-replication-slot WAL retention warnings begin on ledger-db.
ledger-db WARN: disk usage 90% on /var/lib/postgresql/data — the first observable sign of the causal chain, ~1.5h before any deployment.
dep-6203 payment-service v6.0.0 'New UPI mandate flow' (new ledger entry type MANDATE_HOLD) deployed — the only change anywhere in the window.
payment-service error rate still at baseline (~0.19-0.29%) through the 14:56:00Z bucket; onset therefore falls inside 14:56-15:00Z.
First payment-service error: 'ledger write failed: ERROR: could not extend file: No space left on device' (354 occurrences follow); error rate jumps to ~60.15% for the 15:00:00Z bucket.
order-service independently begins failing: 'INSERT INTO orders failed: No space left on device' (236 occurrences).
ledger-db internal storage exhaustion: 153 PANICs writing pg_wal (xlogtemp) 'No space left on device'.
ledger-db further PANICs extending data files under base/.
Incident INC-012 reported by on-call SRE; rollback of payment-service v6.0.0 initiated.
Latest data: payment-service error rate remains 59-64% — service has not recovered, consistent with the untouched exhausted shared volume.

recommended_actions.action: Immediately free space on ledger-db's data volume (priority mitigation): drop/disable the inactive replication slot retaining WAL and run a WAL/space reclamation, then verify disk_used_pct has dropped below ~80% on /var/lib/postgresql/data for the ledger-db component.
recommended_actions.rationale: ledger-db itself is PANIC-ing on pg_wal and data-file extension (F10) after crossing 90% at 13:10Z / 98% at 14:48Z (F9); the retained WAL from the inactive replication slot is the mechanism matching HIST-114 (F6, F17). This is the only action that addresses the actual cause.

recommended_actions.action: Treat the payment-service v6.0.0 rollback as non-curative and keep it reverted only for safety; do not expect recovery from it. Re-verify service health after the disk reclamation above.
recommended_actions.rationale: v6.0.0 was already rolled back at 15:12Z yet error rate stayed 59-64% to 16:59Z (F7, F13), confirming the fault predates and outlives the deploy (H4).

recommended_actions.action: Add monitoring/alerting on ledger-db capacity: alert at 80% disk_used_pct and on any inactive replication slot retaining WAL for more than N hours; wire disk_used_pct and replication_lag_ms into a dashboard for all four writer services.
recommended_actions.rationale: The fill was visible as WARN log lines from 13:10:01Z onward but never triggered a mitigation before hard failure at 15:01Z (F9, F10); the pre-90% trajectory was not tracked by any metric (data gap).

recommended_actions.action: Verify blast radius and recovery across the shared datastore: check order-service, portfolio-service and settlement-service for 'No space left on device' errors and confirm they recover once ledger-db space is reclaimed; also inspect api-gateway, kafka and bank-partner-api for unreviewed impact.
recommended_actions.rationale: order-service already showed identical storage failures from 15:00:42Z (F11) and all four writer services share ledger-db (F4, F16); other components were not fully examined.

recommended_actions.action: Confirm whether payment-service v6.0.0's MANDATE_HOLD flow added meaningful ledger-db write volume, and if so re-deploy v6.0.0 only after ledger-db has headroom and a per-client insert-rate/WAL-generation watch is in place.
recommended_actions.rationale: No insert-rate or write-volume metric was ever retrieved, so v6.0.0's contribution to fill rate is unquantified; it cannot currently be excluded as a minor accelerator (F1, F13, gap list).

recommended_actions.action: Harden the shared postgres: enforce replication-slot hygiene (auto-drop or alert on inactive slots), set max_slot_wal_keep_size, and add a recurring capacity-review process for ledger-db's data volume.
recommended_actions.rationale: HIST-114 was the identical failure mode ('ledger-db disk full from retained WAL', inactive replication slot) on 2025-04-18 (F6, F17); a repeat is evidence of missing preventive control.

data_gaps: Per-component telemetry for ledger-db and kafka (disk_used_pct, write-failure counters, connection/refused errors, IOPS throttling) was never queried, and no metric baseline before 14:46Z was compared — so the disk-fill trajectory rests on log-derived WARN values (90%/95%/98%) rather than an independent metric series.

No deployment or config history was retrieved for ledger-db, kafka, user-db or redis-cache individually; the 'all services' query for the window returned only dep-6203, but per-component release history is not enumerated.

No tool call could read ledger-db's schema / ledger_entry_type enum directly, so MANDATE_HOLD's acceptance status cannot be positively confirmed — only that no DB-side migration exists (F15) and no enum/type error pattern appears in logs (F8).
No write-volume or insert-rate metric per client service was retrieved, so it cannot be quantified whether v6.0.0's MANDATE_HOLD flow increased ledger-db write volume before 15:00Z.
Onset resolution is bounded only to the 14:56-15:00Z window (240s bucket plus first ERROR log at 15:00:26Z); no finer-grained error-rate point was obtained.

Blast radius is potentially under-counted: api-gateway, redis-cache, kafka and bank-partner-api were never queried; settlement-service returned 0 WARN/ERROR logs, and only payment-service, order-service and ledger-db were confirmed degrading.

Tool failures limited coverage: query_logs/get_deployments for 'ledger-service' failed (not_found) and query_metrics(ledger-db, error_rate) failed (not_found), because ledger-db exposes no error_rate metric.
what_would_change_the_conclusion: Evidence that ledger-db disk usage was NOT the constraint — e.g. a ledger-db disk_used_pct metric showing ample free space at ~15:00Z — would undermine H1 and shift weight to the deploy-driven hypotheses (H2/H3).
Discovery of a failed or partial schema migration / enum registration for the MANDATE_HOLD ledger entry type would support H3 (currently rejected) despite the storage-error signature.

Proof that errors are confined to payment-service and that order-service/other writers fail for an unrelated reason would undercut the shared-datastore blast radius and re-open a payment-service-specific cause.
Recovery without any disk reclamation (e.g. error rate returning to baseline at 15:12Z with no space freed) would contradict H4 and point back to the rollback curing the fault, reviving H2.
Evidence that the disk fill accelerated sharply starting exactly at deployment time (14:46Z) with a measurable insert-rate spike would promote H2 from coincidence/accelerator to primary trigger.
